text: An apocryphal story is one repeated as fact even though it probably never happened — widely believed, never verified. The word comes from the Apocrypha, books left out of the official Bible because their authenticity was doubted. Here it flags the bloodthirsty Genghis quote that still gets recycled in leadership talks: the writer passes it on while warning that it may never have left the Khan's mouth.

To ascribe a result to something is to name it as the cause — to assign it the credit or the blame. It hints that this is a judgement rather than a proven fact, which is why art historians ascribe an unsigned painting to a particular artist. The article's whole argument sits inside the word: Genghis would have ascribed his conquests to his own genius, while Jared Diamond ascribes them to the weather.

Belligerent means spoiling for a fight: aggressive, hostile, looking for the argument rather than a way round it. It comes from the Latin for waging war, and in strict legal use a belligerent is a country actually at war — news reports call the two sides in a conflict the belligerents. Here it describes a personality voters apparently like in a leader, even though avoiding fights is one of the things that made Seretse Khama succeed.

This is not the bar you lean on or the bar that blocks a door. Used as a small linking word before a noun, bar simply means except for or apart from — all the guests came bar one. So bar the odd apocryphal quote means everything of Genghis's is lost apart from that one doubtful line.

In this set phrase the odd does not mean strange — it means the occasional, the one that turns up now and then. You will meet it constantly in British writing: he takes the odd day off, there is the odd mistake. The odd quote here means the occasional stray quote that survived.

Chap is casual British English for a man or fellow, roughly what an American would call a guy. It is mild and a bit old-fashioned, which is the joke here: calling the conqueror of half of Eurasia a pretty decisive chap deliberately undersells him for comic effect.

Macho describes an aggressive, showy kind of masculinity — tough talk, no visible doubt, strength on display. It came into English from Spanish, where macho simply means male. It is almost always a mild insult, and it is one here: the macho executives who want Genghis Khan's leadership tips are being gently mocked.

A horde is a large, fast-moving, loosely organised crowd — and the word entered English precisely to describe Mongol armies, from a Turkic word for a nomad camp. Do not confuse it with hoard, which means a stash of hidden treasure and sounds identical. The Mongol horde was devastatingly mobile because every warrior had spare horses to switch to.

The steppe is the enormous belt of flat, treeless grassland that runs across Eurasia from Hungary to Mongolia — too dry for forest, too wet for desert, perfect for grazing animals. It is why the Mongols were horsemen rather than farmers. The word is pronounced exactly like step and has nothing to do with stairs.

Cut a tree across and you see rings: one new ring of wood is added each year, and a wet year grows a wide ring while a dry year grows a narrow one. Because trees in the same region all respond to the same weather, scientists can match overlapping patterns from living trees, old beams and buried logs to build a year-by-year climate record going back thousands of years. That science is called dendrochronology, and a dendrochronologist is the person who does it — the joke being that Genghis had no way of knowing he had been handed unusually rainy decades.

The Pulitzer Prize is the most prestigious American award for journalism, literature and history, funded by the newspaper publisher Joseph Pulitzer and announced every spring at Columbia University. Calling Jared Diamond Pulitzer-prizewinning is shorthand for saying he is a serious, top-rank writer, not a management guru. He won it for Guns, Germs and Steel.

To nourish something is to feed it with what it needs to grow and stay strong — usually food, sometimes an idea or a hope. The related noun is nutrition and the adjective is nourishing. More rain meant more grass, and more grass meant more sheep's milk to nourish the warriors, which is a very literal chain of food.

A warlord is a military strongman who controls territory by force of arms rather than by law or election — his authority is his private army. The word turns up in reporting on Afghanistan, Somalia and the collapse of the Chinese republic in the 1920s. Saying Genghis might have been just another warlord means he might have ruled a valley instead of half a continent.

Charismatic means having charisma: a personal magnetism that makes people want to listen and follow, hard to define and impossible to fake for long. It comes from the Greek for a gift freely given. The article's point is that charisma cannot be the explanation for Christianity, because thousands of other preachers had it too and their movements went nowhere.

A gospel is the account of Jesus's life and teaching — the four in the New Testament are named for Matthew, Mark, Luke and John — and by extension a person's core message. The word is Old English for good news. It also survives in everyday speech: take something as gospel means to treat it as unquestionably true.

A millennium is a thousand years, and millennia is its plural — two millennia ago means roughly 2,000 years ago. Note the spelling with two l's and two n's, from the Latin mille for thousand and annus for year. The same root gives you millipede and annual.

An apostle is one of the early followers sent out to spread Christianity, from a Greek word meaning one who is sent. Paul was the most consequential of them: he never met Jesus in life but wrote much of the New Testament and, as the article notes, deliberately reshaped the message so that non-Jews could join. In ordinary use, an apostle of something is its most devoted promoter.

A creed is a set of beliefs stated as a package — originally a formal declaration of religious faith, from the Latin credo, meaning I believe. It has widened to cover any guiding set of principles, religious or not, as in a political creed. Paul adapting his creed means he adjusted what the new religion demanded of its converts.

To colonise a place is to take control of it, settle it and run it for the benefit of the home country. From the sixteenth century onward European powers colonised most of Africa, Asia and the Americas, which is how Christianity reached every continent. The British spelling uses an s where American English writes colonized.

A polymath is someone genuinely expert in many different fields — Leonardo da Vinci is the stock example — from the Greek for having learned much. Polymathic is the adjective. Jared Diamond earns it honestly: he has published serious work in physiology, ornithology, geography and history.

Rollicking means boisterously enjoyable — fast, lively, high-spirited. A rollicking read is a book that carries you along rather than one you slog through, and reviewers use the word constantly. Watch out for the British noun, though: to give someone a rollicking means to tell them off.

To ponder something is to think it over slowly and seriously, turning it about in your mind rather than answering straight away. The root is the Latin for to weigh, which is exactly the feeling: you are weighing an idea. Pondering why leaders are necessary signals that Diamond stops to examine an assumption most books skip.

Here a clearing is not an act of tidying but a place: an open patch of ground inside a forest where the trees have been cut or never grew. In dense highland New Guinea it is the only space big enough for a hundred people to gather. It is the village equivalent of a town square.

To discern something is to make it out — to detect a thing that is faint, hidden or hard to separate from its background, whether with your eyes or your judgement. The adjective discernible means detectable at all, which is why the Danish study found no discernible effect when a board member died: the researchers looked and there was nothing there to see.

A natural experiment is a piece of real life that accidentally does what a laboratory experiment would do: something outside the researchers' control splits people into groups for reasons unconnected to whatever is being measured. You cannot assign countries a leader at random, but you can treat a leader's sudden death as a coin flip and compare what happened next. Economists, epidemiologists and political scientists lean on the method constantly, and the catch is always the same — the accident has to be genuinely unrelated to the thing you are studying.

To devise something is to work out a way of doing it — to invent a plan, a method or a trick that did not exist before. It is close to design, and shares a root with device. Devising a natural experiment means cleverly finding a situation in the real world that answers your question.

The head of government is whoever actually runs a country day to day — a prime minister in Britain or India, a chancellor in Germany, the president in America. It is deliberately distinguished from the head of state, the ceremonial figure who represents the nation, which in Britain is the monarch. In presidential systems one person is both, which is why the phrase sounds odd to American ears.

Variance is the statistician's word for spread: how far the individual results scatter from the average, rather than where the average sits. Two classes can share the same mean score while one has everyone near 75 and the other has half at 50 and half at 100 — same average, wildly different variance. That gap is the whole finding here: leaders' deaths left average growth untouched but blew the spread wide open, which is what you would see if individual leaders matter a great deal.

An autocracy is a system where one person holds power without meaningful checks — no independent courts, no real elections, no legislature that can say no. The Greek roots mean self-rule, in the sense of ruling by oneself. It matters to the finding because an autocrat's death changes everything, whereas a democracy's institutions carry on regardless of who dies.

To constrain is to hold something within limits, so unconstrained means with nothing holding it back. In politics the constraints are the concrete machinery that can block a leader: a court, a parliament, a free press, a term limit. Leaders with more unconstrained power can do more good and more damage, which is exactly why the effect showed up in autocracies.

To cast light on something is to make it clearer or better understood — the image is shining a lamp into a dark corner. You will see it, and its cousin shed light on, throughout serious writing. Applying the same death-in-office method to company bosses casts light on how much a CEO matters.

A company's board of directors is the small group elected by shareholders to oversee the business: it hires and fires the chief executive and approves big decisions, but does not run things day to day. A board member sits on that body, often part-time and often on several boards at once. The contrast is the point of the Danish study — losing the CEO cost real profits, losing a supervisor of the CEO cost nothing measurable.

Fine-grained means detailed down to the small parts, as opposed to coarse or broad-brush. The image comes from wood and stone, where a fine grain means the particles are tiny and the surface smooth. A fine-grained sense of how to lead means the specifics of particular careers, not just the statistical averages.

Obscure has two senses and this is the less familiar one: not famous, unnoticed, that nobody has heard of. The other sense is hard to understand, and as a verb to obscure something is to hide it from view. Botswana in 1966 was obscure in the first sense — a poor country almost nobody outside Africa could place on a map.

Dismal means gloomy and depressing, with a strong hint of hopelessness — dismal weather, a dismal performance, dismal prospects. It comes from a medieval Latin phrase for evil days. Economics is nicknamed the dismal science, a jab from the nineteenth century that economists have never shaken off.

Strife is bitter conflict — fighting, feuding, violent disagreement within a group or country. It is related to strive, and you will meet it most often in the set phrases civil strife and ethnic strife. The bloody strife that gripped post-colonial Africa means the coups and civil wars that followed independence across the continent.

Post-colonial describes the period after a colonised country wins independence, and the problems peculiar to it: borders drawn by outsiders, institutions built to extract rather than govern, and ethnic groups thrown together inside one new state. For most of Africa that period starts in the 1950s and 1960s. Botswana is the famous exception to how badly it usually went.

Struck here is the past tense of strike in its prospecting sense: to hit a valuable deposit while digging or drilling. Strike oil and strike gold are the classic forms, and strike it rich grew out of them. Botswana struck diamonds means it found them under its own ground, not that it hit anything.

Owning the surface of a piece of land and owning the minerals buried under it are two separate legal rights, and they can belong to two different owners. In most countries, including Britain and nearly all of Africa, the valuable material underground belongs to the state by default; across much of the United States it belongs to whoever owns the surface, which is why American farmers sign drilling leases and collect royalties. Khama's decision to give Botswana's diamond rights to the state rather than to the tribe above them sent the money to the whole country and left no group a prize worth fighting for.

The civil service is the permanent professional staff who actually run a government — the tax collectors, statisticians, health inspectors and clerks — as distinct from the politicians, who come and go with elections. Civil servants are supposed to be hired on merit and to serve whoever wins. A clean civil service means one where jobs are not handed out to relatives and officials do not demand bribes, which is rarer and more valuable than it sounds.

Grounded in something means firmly rooted in it and shaped by it — not the grounded that means banned from going out, and not an aeroplane stuck on the tarmac. A person who is grounded is also sensible and unpretentious, and both senses are working here. Khama had an Oxford education but stayed grounded in the traditions of home, right down to the bag of dried caterpillars.

Apartheid was South Africa's system of enforced racial segregation from 1948 to the early 1990s: where you could live, work, study and whom you could marry were all fixed by an official racial classification, and the black majority could not vote. The word is Afrikaans for apartness and is said roughly uh-PART-hate. Botswana sat right next door, which made Khama's refusal to pick a public fight with his powerful neighbour a genuinely difficult choice.

To loathe something is to hate it with disgust — a stronger and more physical word than dislike. The adjective loathsome describes something repulsive. Note that the verb loathe ends in the soft th sound, while the adjective loath, meaning unwilling, is a different word entirely.

To pick a fight is to start a quarrel deliberately, usually with someone who was not bothering you. The phrase carries a clear judgement: the fight was avoidable and you chose it. Good leaders, the article suggests, avoid picking fights with their neighbours — while plenty of voters seem to want exactly the opposite.

Tribal literally means belonging to a tribe, but in political writing it has taken on a second, critical sense: loyal to your own group above everything, judging arguments by who makes them rather than whether they are right. A tribal leader in this sense is one who governs for his own side alone. The article is playing both senses against each other, since Khama's achievement was refusing to be tribal about the diamonds under his own tribe's land.

Scorn is contempt mixed with a kind of mockery — not just thinking something is wrong but thinking it beneath you. To be scornful of expertise is to treat experts as fools worth sneering at rather than as people who might know something. The related verb is scorn and the sharper cousin is disdain.

Populism is politics built on a clash between the ordinary people and a corrupt elite, with the leader claiming to be the people's only true voice. Nationalism puts one's own nation first and treats outsiders and foreign bodies with suspicion. Bolted together, populist nationalism names the political style that has surged worldwide since the 2010s, and the article's uncomfortable observation is that voters choose it knowingly.

To pin something down is to fix it precisely so it stops slipping away from you — the image is a pinned butterfly that can no longer move. It is used constantly for elusive ideas and vague answers: hard to pin down, pin him down on a date. Pinning down what makes a good leader is hard because the answer keeps depending on circumstances.

Tenacity is the quality of holding on and refusing to let go — persistence in the face of difficulty. The adjective is tenacious, and the Latin root tenere, to hold, also gives you tenant and retain. The article's warning is about dose: tenacity is a virtue right up to the point where it hardens into plain stubbornness.

A soft touch is someone too easily persuaded, talked round or taken advantage of — the person everyone asks for money because they never say no. It is a mild criticism, not a compliment. Here it is the excessive dose of compassion, just as stubbornness is the excessive dose of tenacity.

Loopy is informal for slightly crazy or unhinged, and loopiness is the noun. Pairing it with vision is the joke: a leader is supposed to see a future nobody else can see yet, but the same trait one notch too far is simply talking nonsense. Nothing to do with loops of rope or code.

A dose is the measured quantity of a medicine you take — and the reason the word carries weight is that almost any drug that heals in the right dose will poison you in a larger one. The article borrows that logic for character traits: courage, compassion and vision are not simply good, they are good in the appropriate dose. A useful idea to keep, since it applies to almost every virtue.

Not the round kind here. A sphere is an area of life or activity with its own rules and its own people — the political sphere, the private sphere, the public sphere. Politics, business and other spheres means all the different arenas where somebody has to choose a leader.

Nothing to do with alcohol here. To do something soberly is to do it seriously and clear-headedly, without excitement or wishful thinking, which is the older sense of sober — serious and restrained. Choosing leaders soberly means judging them on evidence rather than on how thrilling their promises sound.

A conman is a swindler who takes your money by first winning your trust — con is short for confidence, so a confidence trick is one that works only because you believed in him. The verb is to con someone. Rejecting the conmen who promise instant golden ages means refusing leaders whose pitch is too good to be true.

A golden age is a past or future period imagined as a peak of prosperity, peace and achievement — the Golden Age of Athens, the golden age of Hollywood. The phrase comes from Greek myth, where the golden age was the first and happiest era of humanity. Promising an instant golden age is the oldest sales pitch in politics, and the article's point is that it should be a warning sign, not a selling point.

Eurasia is Europe and Asia treated as the single landmass they physically are — there is no sea between them, only the convention of the Ural mountains. Geographers and historians use the word when the split into two continents would hide what they are describing. The Mongol empire is the classic case: it stretched from Korea to Hungary without ever crossing an ocean.

Genghis Khan, born around 1162, united the warring Mongol tribes and built the largest contiguous land empire in history, stretching across most of Eurasia by the time his successors were done. Khan is a title meaning ruler, not a surname, and the name is usually said GENG-gis or JENG-gis. He is the standard shorthand for ruthless, decisive leadership, which is exactly the reputation this article sets out to complicate.

Jared Diamond is an American geographer and historian, best known for Guns, Germs and Steel, who argues that the broad shape of history is set by geography and environment rather than by the character of peoples. Profits, Prophets, Coaches and Kings is his book on leadership, reviewed here. British publications write Dr Diamond on later mentions where an American one would write Diamond.

Diamond's 1997 book, which won the Pulitzer Prize, asks why Europeans ended up conquering the Americas rather than the other way round. His answer is geography: Eurasia happened to have the best domesticable plants and animals, which brought farming, dense cities, the diseases those cities breed, and eventually the steel and firearms of the title. It is one of the most argued-over popular history books of the last thirty years.

Seretse Khama was the first president of Botswana, from independence in 1966 until his death in 1980, and is the usual answer to the question of whether one leader can change a country's fate. He was an Oxford-educated tribal heir whose marriage to a white Englishwoman had him exiled by the British for years. He is remembered for handing the diamond wealth to the state and for stepping down within the rules he had written.

Botswana is a landlocked country in southern Africa, sitting on the Kalahari desert just north of South Africa, with a population of about 2.5 million. At independence it was among the poorest places on earth; diamonds and unusually honest government have since made it one of Africa's richest per person, and it has held free elections continuously ever since. Economists cite it constantly as the exception that proves resource wealth need not be a curse.

New Guinea is the huge tropical island north of Australia, split between Papua New Guinea and Indonesia, and its mountainous interior held communities that had almost no contact with the outside world until the twentieth century. Its extraordinary variety of small, isolated societies is why anthropologists go there. Diamond did his early fieldwork on the island and draws on it throughout his books.
